Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

wild adjective

of children: unruly, out of hand

also running wild, boisterous, frisky, go wild, run wild

classical

Hor. S. 1.3.134: puerī; Verg. E. 2.64: capella (Lewis & Short)

lascīvus, lascīva, lascīvum

frisky, playful, wild

(vōx plērumque poētica: Verg., Hor., Ov.)

In a good sense, of kids, children and young animals that frisk and play (Lewis & Short). It also means lewd, lustful (Ovid, Martial), so with children the verb lascīvīre, which has no such sense, is the safer choice.

Other words

  • lascīviō, lascīvīre, lascīviī, lascīvītum — run wild, frisk, play the fool

    verb, fourth conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.63: licet lascīvīre, dum nihil metuās (Lewis & Short); Liv. 2.29.9; Sen. Ep. 56.9

    Of people who run riot when nothing holds them back (Cicero, Livy), and of a lamb frisking off (Ov. M. 7.321).

  • petulāns, petulantis — pert, cheeky, unruly

    also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.305 (Lewis & Short); Phaedr. 1.2.20: turba petulāns

    Forward and saucy, out to provoke; stronger than lascīvus, and a reproach.

Examples

  • numquam vacat lascīvīre districtīs

    the busy never have time to run wildSen. Ep. 56.9

  • illae timōre positō certātim adnatant lignumque suprā turba petulāns īnsilit

    putting their fear aside they swim up, racing each other, and the cheeky crowd jumps up onto the logPhaedr. 1.2.19–20

See also noisy, wild.

SourcesLewis & Short: lascivus · Lewis & Short: lascivio · Lewis & Short: petulans

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-seneca-epistulae, loci-phaedrus), checked against the editions named there. Cicero as Lewis & Short quotes him.
